paragraphs: The paper examines how to describe the losses a predictive model is likely to incur after deployment. Conformal prediction addresses this problem with distribution-free guarantees and can work even when the model’s internal details are unavailable. The authors argue that the frequentist interpretation underlying these guarantees restricts how they can be used.

Their approach revisits the central ingredients of conformal prediction from a Bayesian perspective. This changes the way uncertainty about future losses is represented and interpreted. The proposed practical alternative uses Bayesian quadrature, placing that method at the center of a framework for describing a model’s likely test-time behavior.

The stated contribution is both conceptual and methodological: a critique of how existing guarantees should be understood, together with an alternative that offers interpretable guarantees and a richer picture of possible losses. This matters when a deployment decision requires understanding the range of likely outcomes, beyond the particular assurance supplied by a conventional conformal procedure.
icml-2025-conformal-prediction-as-bayesi.tldr: The paper reinterprets conformal prediction through Bayesian reasoning and proposes Bayesian quadrature for richer, interpretable descriptions of test-time losses.

paragraphs: Universal approximation results describe the ability of a model family to approximate functions. This paper develops a constructive version for learning systems whose feature maps satisfy joint-group-equivariance. Constructive means that the result supplies a closed-form expression for the distribution of model parameters, using a mathematical object called the ridgelet transform.

Joint-group-equivariance broadens the symmetry framework beyond classical group-equivariance. In particular, the authors place fully connected networks within this broader class even though they are not group-equivariant in the classical sense. Using group representation theory, the paper brings shallow and deep networks into one approximation framework, connecting results that had previously been established through different arguments.

The authors apply their theorem to arbitrary-depth joint-equivariant machines, fully connected networks, and group-convolutional networks. They also establish constructive universality for a two-layer network built with quadratic forms, whose universality had not previously been known. The contribution is a common mathematical account of approximation across these architectures, including an explicit parameter description that makes the theorem constructive.
icml-2025-deep-ridgelet-transform-and-un.tldr: A constructive theorem uses joint-group-equivariance and ridgelet transforms to unify universal approximation results for shallow and deep networks.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image hashing learns compact discrete representations for retrieval without requiring labeled images. These representations support efficient search and reduce storage needs. The paper argues that methods relying only on visual relationships within their training images have limited semantic information available, which can restrict how well their codes distinguish relevant image content.

DUH-EG introduces external textual knowledge as an additional source of guidance. It first selects representative nouns from a text database while reducing redundancy among them. Images are then matched to those nouns to obtain external features. This supplies semantic information that complements the visual structure already present in the unlabeled image collection.

A bidirectional contrastive learning mechanism encourages agreement between hash codes associated with the internal and external representation spaces. The aim is to preserve useful distinctions from both sources in the space where binary codes are compared. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art hashing methods, supporting external semantic guidance as a useful addition to unsupervised image retrieval.
icml-2025-deep-unsupervised-hashing-via-.tldr: DUH-EG improves unsupervised image hashing by combining internal visual structure with semantic guidance from an external text database.

paragraphs: The paper studies distributed optimization on the Stiefel manifold, a constrained optimization setting used in applications including principal component analysis and neural network robustness. The existing Landing algorithm avoids expensive retraction operations associated with manifold optimization. The authors extend that computational advantage to distributed learning, where communication between participants creates an additional cost.

Their algorithm, EF-Landing, combines communication compression with error feedback. Compression reduces the information exchanged, while error feedback accounts for compression errors. The analysis establishes convergence and constraint feasibility while reducing communication overhead. It also shows that the method retains the same asymptotic linear speedup convergence rate as existing methods that communicate without compression.

The theoretical treatment covers both deterministic and stochastic optimization, including gradient descent and momentum-based variants. A further extension handles block-wise Stiefel manifolds, allowing the method to accommodate structured constraints. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. Together, these results show how avoiding costly manifold operations and reducing distributed communication can be addressed within one optimization approach.
icml-2025-distributed-retraction-free-an.tldr: EF-Landing reduces communication in distributed Stiefel-manifold optimization while avoiding retractions and preserving established asymptotic convergence speedups.

paragraphs: PROTAC molecules connect two molecular fragments through a linker, and designing that connection is an important challenge in targeted protein degradation. Diffusion models offer a way to generate linkers, but existing models are commonly trained on small molecules. Their training distribution therefore differs from the chemical space of the PROTACs they are intended to produce.

The paper introduces DAD-PROTAC to address this mismatch through domain adaptation. Its central tool is density ratio estimation, which captures differences between the small-molecule and PROTAC distributions. The target score estimator is separated into an existing pretrained score function and a lightweight correction term that adjusts it toward the target domain.

This decomposition enables efficient fine-tuning without retraining the entire model. It responds to a difficulty identified by the authors: directly fine-tuning on limited PROTAC data can overfit and generalize poorly. Experiments report superior generation of high-quality linkers. The result supports adapting the model’s generative guidance to PROTAC chemistry while retaining the useful information learned from the larger source domain.
icml-2025-domain-adapted-diffusion-model.tldr: DAD-PROTAC adapts a pretrained molecular diffusion model with a lightweight density-ratio-based correction to improve PROTAC linker generation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to control pretrained diffusion models during sampling, including when combining multiple models. Standard classifier-free guidance mixes conditional and unconditional scores using a heuristic. The authors identify a problem with this approach: the mixture does not approximate the desired intermediate distributions, motivating additional correction during the generation process.

Feynman-Kac Correctors provide a weighted simulation scheme derived by accounting for terms in the relevant partial differential equations. The framework targets sequences of distributions formed through annealing, geometric averaging, or products of pretrained model distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo resampling algorithms implement the scheme and use additional inference-time computation to improve sampling quality.

The authors demonstrate the approach in three settings: amortized sampling through inference-time temperature annealing, molecule generation with multiple objectives, and classifier-free guidance for text-to-image generation. These applications connect the mathematical correction to practical ways of controlling existing generative models. The reported improvements support treating intermediate sampling distributions explicitly when adjusting or combining pretrained models.
icml-2025-feynman-kac-correctors-in-diff.tldr: Feynman-Kac Correctors use weighted simulation and resampling to improve principled inference-time control and composition of pretrained diffusion models.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes compare neural representations by testing whether they can be functionally aligned through model stitching. A common interpretation is that a successful connection indicates that the representations contain similar information. This paper challenges that inference by showing that functional compatibility can occur even when the underlying representations capture very different information.

The authors first demonstrate successful stitching between discriminative models with substantially different biases. They then extend the investigation to representations from models trained on entirely different tasks and data modalities. Even clustered random noise can be stitched into models trained on MNIST or ImageNet, making the gap between functional alignment and informational similarity especially clear.

These examples matter for interpreting what a successful stitching experiment establishes. The result shows that the ability to make representations work together does not, by itself, demonstrate shared informational content. The authors therefore call for greater care with functional similarity measures and for comparison methods that directly capture informational similarity. Their contribution concerns the conclusions researchers can draw from these experiments.
icml-2025-functional-alignment-can-misle.tldr: Successful model stitching can connect representations with very different information, so functional alignment alone does not establish informational similarity.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations can describe volumes with strong expressive capacity and lower memory use than voxel grids. Their usual training procedures involve nonconvex optimization, which can be slow and sensitive to starting conditions and hyperparameters. This paper introduces GA-Planes, a family of volume representations inspired by Geometric Algebra that permits convex training.

GA-Planes generalizes representations that store features in combinations of tensor basis elements and pass those features through a neural decoder. The framework can be adapted for either convex or nonconvex optimization, depending on the inverse problem. This flexibility connects a broad representation family with different choices about how its parameters are fitted.

In two dimensions, the authors prove an equivalence to matrix factorization combining low rank with low resolution. For fitting a natural image, that formulation outperforms a classic low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition. In three dimensions, the models show competitive expressiveness, size, and ease of optimization across radiance field reconstruction, 3D segmentation, and video segmentation. These findings connect the mathematical formulation to practical representation tasks.
icml-2025-geometric-algebra-planes-conve.tldr: GA-Planes offers a flexible family of implicit volume representations that supports convex training and competitive performance across several reconstruction and segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Generating video from earlier frames requires a model to use a history whose length may vary. The paper identifies two obstacles to applying classifier-free guidance in this setting: some architectures accept only a fixed amount of conditioning, and dropping history during training in the usual guidance style performs poorly in the authors’ experiments.

The proposed Diffusion Forcing Transformer combines an architecture with a theoretically grounded training objective that allows conditioning on flexible numbers of history frames. This capability enables a family of methods called History Guidance. Its simplest version already produces substantial improvements in video generation quality and in consistency between frames over time.

A more advanced version applies history guidance across both time and frequency. The authors report improved motion dynamics, compositional generalization to histories outside the training distribution, and stable generation of extremely long videos. The approach makes flexible use of previous frames part of both model training and sampling guidance, helping connect immediate visual quality with coherent behavior across a longer sequence.
icml-2025-history-guided-video-diffusion.tldr: History Guidance uses a diffusion architecture that accepts variable-length frame histories to improve video quality, temporal consistency, and long video generation.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion generates images and videos in a compressed representation supplied by an autoencoder. This paper examines whether that representation is well suited to the diffusion process. Spectral analysis reveals unusually strong high-frequency components in modern autoencoder latent spaces, particularly when the compressed representation has a large number of channels.

The authors hypothesize that these components interfere with diffusion’s coarse-to-fine synthesis process. They propose a scale-equivariance regularizer for the decoder to align the frequency behavior of latent representations and RGB outputs. The method targets the interaction between the autoencoder and diffusion model, extending attention beyond reconstruction quality or the size of the diffusion backbone.

The change requires minimal code modifications and up to 20,000 autoencoder fine-tuning steps. Reported results include a 19% reduction in FID for ImageNet-1K image generation at 256-by-256 resolution and at least a 44% reduction in FVD for Kinetics-700 video generation. These improvements support the usefulness of the regularizer, while the proposed interference mechanism is presented as a hypothesis.
icml-2025-improving-the-diffusability-of.tldr: A scale-equivariance regularizer makes autoencoder latents more suitable for diffusion, improving reported image and video generation quality with limited fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces in-context denoising as a way to study how attention relates to associative memory. In this task, a query is refined using information provided by context tokens. Through a Bayesian analysis and empirical evidence, the authors show that a single-layer transformer can optimally solve certain restricted versions of the denoising problem.

They interpret a trained attention layer as performing one gradient descent step on the energy landscape of a context-aware dense associative memory, also called a modern Hopfield network. In this interpretation, the context tokens supply the memories, while the query token supplies the initial state from which the update begins.

That single update produces better solutions than exactly retrieving a context token or settling at a spurious local minimum. This gives a concrete example in which associative memory is useful beyond straightforward memory retrieval. The finding strengthens the connection between attention and associative memory while providing a specific account of how contextual information can guide computation in a small transformer.
icml-2025-in-context-denoising-with-one-.tldr: For certain restricted denoising problems, one-layer attention achieves Bayesian optimality through an update interpretable as associative-memory gradient descent.

paragraphs: Understanding a reinforcement learning policy one neuron at a time becomes difficult as models grow. This paper instead studies groups of network components that carry out recognizable functions. Its proposed pipeline addresses three connected tasks: encouraging such modules to emerge, finding them within a trained network, and checking what roles they perform.

The authors encourage sparsity and locality in network weights, which leads to functional modules in the policy networks they study. To identify the modules, they extend the Louvain community-detection algorithm with a correlation alignment metric. The extension addresses limitations that standard network analysis methods encounter when applied to neural network architectures.

In two-dimensional and three-dimensional MiniGrid environments, the method consistently reveals separate navigation modules associated with different axes. The authors then intervene directly on network weights before inference to validate the modules’ functions. This links structural groupings to changes in policy behavior and supports functional modules as a useful scale for interpreting the tested reinforcement learning systems.
icml-2025-inducing-detecting-and-charact.tldr: A pipeline encourages, detects, and experimentally validates functional navigation modules in reinforcement learning policy networks.

paragraphs: The paper questions the common practice of taking a model’s final layer as its best general-purpose representation. Earlier layers are often treated as sources of relatively basic features, but the authors find that intermediate layers can contain richer information for downstream tasks. This makes the choice of extraction layer an important part of using pretrained representations.

To explain these differences, the authors introduce a unified set of representation-quality measures drawing on information theory, geometry, and stability under input perturbations. The framework examines how individual layers balance compression with preservation of useful signals. It provides a way to characterize why an embedding from the middle of a network can outperform its final-layer counterpart.

Experiments cover 32 text-embedding tasks and investigate multiple architectures, including transformers and state-space models, across language and vision domains. Intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features in the reported study. The results support considering mid-depth representations when building downstream systems, while the proposed metrics offer a framework for analyzing where useful information resides within a model.
icml-2025-layer-by-layer-uncovering-hidd.tldr: Intermediate model layers provide stronger features in the reported experiments, and a unified metric framework helps explain their representational advantages.

paragraphs: When classifiers influence lending, hiring, or admissions, people may change their features to obtain favorable predictions. Strategic classification studies this response, usually assuming that the cost of changing each feature is already fixed. This paper challenges that assumption by considering how deploying the classifier can itself change the costs people face.

The proposed mechanism is a market for purchasable features. Features that help secure positive predictions attract demand, and competition produces prices. Under this setup, the classifier affects which features people want, while the resulting market determines their cost. Learning therefore involves a connection between the decision rule, strategic behavior, and the prices induced by that behavior.

The authors extend the strategic classification framework to represent this setting, analyze the learning problem, and develop an algorithm for calculating market prices. They also propose a differentiable learning framework and conduct experiments exploring the approach. The contribution is a way to study classifiers whose deployment shapes the economic conditions underlying users’ attempts to change their predictions.
icml-2025-learning-classifiers-that-indu.tldr: The paper extends strategic classification to settings where a classifier creates demand for purchasable features and thereby influences their market prices.

paragraphs: CLIP can lose performance when fine-tuning is followed by evaluation in a different environment. This paper analyzes that problem with a structural causal model. The authors distinguish factors that remain stable across environments from those that vary, and show how including both kinds can produce a prediction mechanism that changes between training and testing.

Their analysis identifies consistency in the mechanism using only invariant factors. They prove the existence of a linear mapping from CLIP embeddings to these factors and show that interventional data can be used to estimate it. They also provide a condition under which the invariant predictor is guaranteed to have low out-of-distribution risk.

The resulting CLIP-ICM framework collects interventional data, estimates a linear projection, and makes predictions in the resulting invariant subspace. Experiments on several out-of-distribution datasets report significant improvements over CLIP. The work connects a causal account of distribution shift with a concrete adaptation procedure, with its risk guarantee depending on the stated condition and its projection estimated through interventions.
icml-2025-learning-invariant-causal-mech.tldr: CLIP-ICM uses interventional data to learn a linear projection onto invariant factors, improving CLIP on several out-of-distribution datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn classifiers that obey specified symmetries exactly within kernel regression. Enforcing invariance can create a computational burden, and the authors explain that familiar approaches either fail to give a polynomial-time solution or do not apply in this setting. The challenge is to combine exact symmetry with efficient computation.

With oracle access to geometric properties of the input space, the authors give a polynomial-time algorithm whose classifier has exact invariances. It achieves the same excess population risk as the original kernel regression problem. The oracle assumption is part of the result: the efficiency claim is established with that geometric information available.

The analysis also addresses efficient computation of invariant bases and kernels for finite groups, even when those groups are prohibitively large. A central mathematical step reformulates invariant learning through infinitely many convex quadratic programs with linear constraints. Using differential geometry, spectral theory, and optimization, the work connects computational tractability with exact symmetry while preserving the stated generalization guarantee.
icml-2025-learning-with-exact-invariance.tldr: Given a geometric oracle, the proposed kernel-learning algorithm achieves exact invariance in polynomial time while preserving the original excess-risk guarantee.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning controllers can produce rapidly fluctuating actions, causing actuator wear, safety risks, and weaker performance in physical systems. This paper identifies two fundamental sources of the problem: noise in observations and a policy function that changes too sharply. LipsNet++ addresses both within a single policy network using separate filtering and control layers.

The Fourier filter layer learns a matrix that retains important observation frequencies while suppressing noise frequencies. The Lipschitz controller layer uses Jacobian regularization to keep the policy’s Lipschitz constant low, encouraging smoother changes in its outputs. These components play roles analogous to the filter and controller in classical control theory.

The authors evaluate LipsNet++ in both simulated and real-world experiments and report state-of-the-art noise robustness and action smoothness. The approach matters because observation quality and policy sensitivity can each contribute to unstable actions. Integrating mechanisms for both into the network provides a direct way to train filtering and smooth control capabilities together within the reinforcement learning policy.
icml-2025-lipsnet-unifying-filter-and-co.tldr: LipsNet++ combines learned frequency filtering with a smooth controller to reduce action fluctuations and improve noise robustness in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A video question-answering system may provide an answer without revealing its reasoning or the video evidence behind it. This paper addresses that interpretability problem in multimodal language models. MSR-ViR integrates modular networks into the answering process so that the system can expose explicit reasoning paths and identify relevant parts of the video.

Its MoST-Grounding network breaks complex questions into steps using tree-structured policies. These steps locate relevant intervals in time and regions in space, producing visually grounded information for the multimodal language model. The resulting reasoning path links the question’s decomposition to the video segments used in constructing an answer.

An alternating self-reflection training strategy jointly optimizes policy generation and the multimodal language model to improve reasoning quality. Experiments on real-world datasets report stronger video understanding, greater reasoning transparency, and explicit localization evidence for answers. The approach makes evidence selection part of the system’s visible reasoning process, giving users more information about how an answer relates to the observed video.
icml-2025-modularized-self-reflected-vid.tldr: MSR-ViR answers video questions through modular reasoning that explicitly locates supporting video evidence and exposes the reasoning path.

paragraphs: Controlling fusion plasma is difficult because its dynamics are complex, data quality is poor, hardware can fail, and experiments can affect the system beyond their own duration. The paper develops a Bayesian optimization approach that operates across multiple timescales, addressing the need to make control decisions while adapting to changing experimental conditions.

The method combines a high-frequency, data-driven dynamics model with a low-frequency Gaussian process. The Gaussian process is updated between experiments and refines predictions from the less reliable dynamics model. This arrangement allows new experimental information to adjust the overall predictive system without relying solely on the existing dynamics model.

The authors evaluate the method for controlling tearing instabilities in the DIII-D tokamak. Offline tests on historical data substantially outperform several baselines. Live experiments in high-performance plasma scenarios prone to instability achieve a 50% success rate, reported as a 117% improvement over historical outcomes. These results provide both retrospective and live experimental evidence for the proposed adaptation strategy in this demanding control setting.
icml-2025-multi-timescale-dynamics-model.tldr: A multi-timescale Bayesian optimization method adapts plasma-control predictions between experiments and achieves a reported 50% success rate in live DIII-D tests.

paragraphs: Repository-level software work requires an agent to find relevant code and reason across context that may exceed a language model’s input capacity. Debugging and feature implementation also expose brittleness in standard autoregressive reasoning. Nemotron-CORTEXA addresses these problems through an agent system with a predefined scaffold for navigating and solving software engineering tasks.

The system introduces a code embedding model that retrieves relevant files more precisely. A localization agent then narrows the retrieval to finer-grained information, improving the context supplied to the language model. The authors also investigate diversity in contextual information and prompt formats, finding that these choices help the model identify and resolve issues more efficiently.

Evaluation uses SWE-bench, which contains tasks derived from real GitHub issues. Nemotron-CORTEXA resolves a larger share of issues at lower cost than the Agentless framework in the reported comparison. The findings emphasize that better code localization and varied solution contexts can improve an agent’s effectiveness on repository tasks, alongside the capabilities of the underlying language model.
icml-2025-nemotron-cortexa-enhancing-llm.tldr: Nemotron-CORTEXA combines precise code retrieval, finer localization, and diverse contexts to resolve more SWE-bench issues at lower cost than Agentless.

paragraphs: Designing proteins that bind strongly to a chosen target remains challenging, especially when extensive laboratory testing is needed. PPDiff approaches this task by jointly generating a binder’s amino acid sequence and three-dimensional structure with a diffusion model. The design process is non-autoregressive and is intended to support arbitrary protein targets.

The underlying Sequence Structure Interleaving Network combines several mechanisms. Interleaved self-attention captures global relationships among amino acids, while nearest-neighbor equivariant graph convolutions capture local interactions in three-dimensional space. Causal attention layers simplify dependencies within the sequence. Together, these components connect sequence-level information with the spatial relationships needed to model a protein complex.

The authors curate PPBench from 706,360 Protein Data Bank complexes, pretrain PPDiff on it, and fine-tune for mini-binder and antigen-antibody complex design. Reported success rates are 50.00% for pretraining, 23.16% for mini-binder design, and 16.89% for antigen-antibody design, with consistent improvements over baseline methods. The results support joint sequence-and-structure generation across these evaluated protein-complex design tasks.
icml-2025-ppdiff-diffusing-in-hybrid-seq.tldr: PPDiff jointly generates protein binder sequences and structures, outperforming baseline methods across the reported pretraining and downstream complex-design tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies personalized federated learning with user-level differential privacy. Users have statistically different data, but their optimal model parameters are assumed to share an unknown low-dimensional representation. The goal is to recover that shared structure and each user’s local representation while keeping excess prediction risk small and satisfying privacy requirements.

The authors propose an efficient private algorithm based on FedRep. Their guarantees accommodate noisy labels and sub-Gaussian user distributions, expanding beyond the Gaussian setting of prior private personalization work. In natural parameter regimes, the privacy error term improves by a factor expressed as roughly dk, up to logarithmic factors, where d and k are the original and representation dimensions.

For binary classification, the paper separately gives an information-theoretic construction with a margin-based accuracy guarantee independent of d. It uses the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform to reduce the effective dimensions of both the shared embedding and users’ data. This establishes that dimension-independent risk bounds are possible under a margin loss in the studied shared-representation setting.
icml-2025-private-model-personalization-.tldr: The paper strengthens private federated personalization guarantees and establishes the possibility of dimension-independent margin-based risk bounds for binary classification.

paragraphs: Language model preference training commonly treats preferences as stable, even though what users favor can change over time. The paper argues that ignoring this drift can produce substantial misalignment. It introduces Non-Stationary Direct Preference Optimisation, or NS-DPO, to make the timing of preference data part of the training objective.

NS-DPO represents changing rewards with a Dynamic Bradley-Terry model. Its practical modification adds one discount parameter to the loss, using exponential weights to emphasize data that is more relevant in time. The authors analyze convergence without assuming that the exact form of preference drift is known, deriving upper bounds on estimation error and regret.

Experiments introduce different levels of drift using established language model reward models and datasets. In these scenarios, NS-DPO remains robust and significantly outperforms algorithms that ignore temporal changes, without sacrificing performance in the stationary cases tested. The findings support temporal weighting as a computationally efficient way to adapt preference optimization when older and newer judgments no longer express the same priorities.
icml-2025-right-now-wrong-then-non-stati.tldr: NS-DPO adds time-based discounting to preference optimization, improving robustness to preference drift in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent can coordinate poorly if it assumes its partner makes rational choices while that partner responds to risk in a biased way. This paper studies that mismatch in multi-agent coordination. It focuses on settings that encourage risky decisions, where an inaccurate model of the partner may be especially consequential.

The proposed Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind framework allows an agent to reason about and adapt to a partner whose risk sensitivity is initially unknown. The work formulates a risk-sensitive coordination problem using cumulative prospect theory. Its central aim is to incorporate the partner’s response to risk into the agent’s model and planning.

Simulation studies compare this approach with an agent that assumes its partner is rational. The authors report significant improvements in team performance, coordination fluency, respect for the partner’s risk preferences, and predictability. These findings establish benefits in the simulated settings. They also suggest potential for coordinating with real-world partners who exhibit similar risk-sensitive biases, with that transfer presented as a prospective implication.
icml-2025-risk-sensitive-theory-of-mind-.tldr: Risk-Sensitive Theory of Mind improves simulated coordination by adapting to a partner’s unknown risk sensitivity.

paragraphs: Graphs are usually represented with discrete node and edge attributes, but the paper draws motivation from the continuous representation of topology available through graph spectra. The authors investigate whether a generation process that reflects this continuity can improve graph modeling. Their proposed framework, Graph Bayesian Flow Networks, emphasizes how topological information develops during generation.

GraphBFN uses continuous counts associated with infinitely repeated sampling from a categorical distribution as its latent representation. This supports a smooth decomposition of topological information within the generative process. The authors also introduce an advanced sampling strategy and new time schedules to address practical obstacles in implementing the framework and improve its performance.

Experiments cover both general graph generation and molecular graph generation. The reported results show consistently superior or competitive performance alongside substantially greater training and sampling efficiency. The contribution connects a continuous latent description with discrete graph outputs, providing an alternative to recent discrete diffusion approaches and evidence that this choice of generative process can offer practical benefits.
icml-2025-smooth-interpolation-for-impro.tldr: GraphBFN uses continuous latent counts to generate discrete graphs smoothly, achieving competitive or better quality with improved training and sampling efficiency.
